changes_in_application_order.reason: Separate device materials from manufacturing consumables; introduce abbreviations by purpose; remove rhetorical importance and universal application claims while preserving numbers and estimate caveats.
changes_in_application_order.before:
Silicon is the substrate of almost every chip that matters, but it is not the only semiconductor in the box, and the polished wafer that arrived at the end of Module 03 is only the beginning of the fab's shopping list. Every one of the ~1,000+ process steps a leading-edge wafer goes through (a **process step** is one pass through one tool: one film deposited, one pattern exposed, one clean) consumes something: a resist, a gas, an acid, a slurry, a sputter target, a precursor, a quartz tube, a photomask. A 300 mm wafer that leaves TSMC N2 at ~$25,000–30,000 (industry estimates; TSMC does not publish) has had thousands of dollars of consumables poured over it and pumped through it, and most of those consumables came from a small number of companies, many of them Japanese, that most people have never heard of.

This module has two halves. **Half A** covers the semiconductors that are not silicon, or not plain silicon: strained SiGe inside every modern transistor, silicon carbide in every 800 V electric-vehicle inverter, gallium nitride in the charger on your desk, gallium arsenide in your phone's radio, indium phosphide in the lasers that carry every bit between GPUs (graphics processing units, the accelerator chips that do AI arithmetic) in an AI cluster, and the 2D materials being tested as the channel material for the 2030s. **Half B** is the consumables supply chain: what a fab burns through, at what purity, from whom, and why a single Japanese chemical plant or one Ukrainian gas purifier can ripple across the world's semiconductor output.

The hard problem in both halves is the same: making something at **part-per-trillion (ppt)** purity (one foreign atom in a million million, the same ratio as one second in 32,000 years) and atomic-scale perfection, reproducibly, at industrial scale, with a **qualification** lock-in so severe that switching vendors mid-node can take a year. Qualification is the 6–18 month campaign of running a new material through a fab's full process flow and proving that yield does not move before it is allowed anywhere near product wafers; once a material is qualified, nobody wants to repeat the campaign.

By the end you should be able to explain why a SiC wafer costs tens of times more than a silicon one, why a GaN charger has no GaN wafer in it, what 18.2 MΩ·cm water is and why a fab needs six cubic metres of it per wafer, why an EUV mask is a mirror, and why one Japanese plant can stop the world's memory output with a customs form.
changes_in_application_order.after:
A chip factory needs two kinds of materials: materials that become part of the finished device, and **consumables** used to manufacture it. Silicon is the main starting surface, or **substrate**, for most chips in this course. Other semiconductors can make better power switches, radio components or light sources. Consumables do different jobs: gases supply atoms for a film, acids clean a surface, and polishing mixtures remove material. Some supply atoms that remain in the chip; much of what enters the factory is removed or recycled after doing its job.

This module follows both groups. **Half A** explains why a designer would choose something other than plain silicon: silicon-germanium (SiGe) to improve a transistor, silicon carbide (SiC) for an 800 V electric-vehicle inverter, gallium nitride (GaN) for a compact charger, gallium arsenide (GaAs) for a phone's radio, or indium phosphide (InP) for a laser in an optical link. Those links carry data between **GPUs**, graphics processing units used as accelerator chips for AI arithmetic. We also look at the 2D materials being tested as transistor channels for the 2030s. The aim is to understand each material's advantage and what it costs to manufacture, rather than to memorize the list.

**Half B** follows the fab's shopping list. A **fab** is a chip factory; a **process step** is one pass through a tool, such as depositing a film, exposing a pattern or cleaning a wafer. A leading-edge wafer goes through ~1,000+ such steps. A 300 mm wafer that leaves TSMC N2 at ~$25,000–30,000 (industry estimates; TSMC does not publish) has had thousands of dollars of consumables poured over it and pumped through it. We will connect each material to its job before asking who supplies it and why replacing that supplier is difficult.

The common challenge is control: the right composition, the right atomic structure, and impurities kept low enough for the particular job. Some impurity limits reach **part-per-trillion (ppt)** levels: one foreign atom in a million million, the same ratio as one second in 32,000 years. The requirement is not identical for every material. A fab must also prove that a new supply works reliably in its process. That **qualification** can mean a 6–18 month campaign through the full manufacturing sequence, checking that the fraction of working chips, or **yield**, does not fall. This is why switching vendors mid-node can take a year even when the replacement has the same chemical name.

By the end you should be able to explain why a SiC wafer costs tens of times more than a silicon one, how a GaN charger can be made from material grown on a silicon wafer, what 18.2 MΩ·cm water means and why a fab needs six cubic metres per wafer, why an EUV mask is a mirror, and how a disruption at one chemical supplier can reach a distant chip factory.

changes_in_application_order.reason: Replace misleading perpetual-battery analogy with charge separation and explain both dimensionality and electron source limitation.
changes_in_application_order.before: > **Intuition: a built-in battery in every unit cell.** In GaN every unit cell is a tiny battery: the Ga and N atoms are arranged so that the centres of positive and negative charge do not coincide (**spontaneous polarization**). Stack a different battery on top, AlGaN, which is also stretched to fit GaN's lattice and so adds a strain-induced (**piezoelectric**) term, and the mismatch between the two leaves a sheet of net positive charge at the interface. That sheet pulls in electrons from wherever it can find them, and they pile up in a layer a few nanometres thick right at the interface, free to move sideways but trapped vertically: a two-dimensional electron gas.
changes_in_application_order.after: > **Intuition: charge gathers at a boundary.** In GaN, the centres of positive and negative charge within the crystal do not quite coincide. This built-in separation is called **spontaneous polarization**. Aluminium gallium nitride (AlGaN) has a different polarization, and stretching it to fit GaN changes that separation further; this strain effect is **piezoelectric polarization**. At the boundary, the two arrangements do not cancel, leaving a net positive sheet of charge. It attracts electrons into a layer a few nanometres thick. They can move along the boundary but are confined across its thickness. That is what “two-dimensional electron gas” means: mobile electrons inside a solid, not a pocket of gaseous material. The polarization creates the attraction; it does not create electrons or supply energy like a battery.

changes_in_application_order.reason: Explain measurement purpose, unit and limit without implying all ions are absent.
changes_in_application_order.before: > **Intuition: resistivity is a live ion meter.** Pure water conducts electricity only through the tiny fraction of its own molecules that split into H+ and OH- ions (about one in ten million). Any dissolved salt adds ions, and every ion carries current, so the resistivity drops. Resistivity is therefore a continuous meter of ion content: 18.2 MΩ·cm means the ions are essentially gone. It says nothing about neutral organic molecules, dissolved silica, bacteria or particles, none of which carry current, and that is why those need their own meters.
changes_in_application_order.after: > **Intuition: resistivity is a live ion meter.** Dissolved salts supply **ions**, atoms or groups of atoms with an electrical charge. Those ions carry current through water, so adding salt lowers its **resistivity**, the material's resistance to current flow after allowing for the measuring cell's size. Even pure water conducts a little: a tiny fraction of its molecules split into H+ and OH- ions (about one in ten million). The target of 18.2 MΩ·cm means the water is close to that pure-water limit, not that every ion has vanished. The unit reads “megohm-centimetres.” This measurement mainly answers “how much ionic contamination is present?” It cannot certify the absence of neutral organic molecules, dissolved silica, bacteria or particles; those need separate measurements.

changes_in_application_order.reason: Replace an ambiguous voltage-absorption analogy with field as voltage change per distance, establishing the causal bridge to the formula.
changes_in_application_order.before: The voltage is held by a **drift region**, a thick, lightly doped layer that absorbs the electric field the way a long insulator absorbs voltage.
changes_in_application_order.after: When the switch is off, a **drift region** spreads the voltage drop through a thick, lightly doped layer. **Electric field** describes how quickly voltage changes with distance: forcing the same voltage drop into a shorter distance means a stronger field. The layer does not use up voltage; it provides enough distance to keep the field below the level that would cause breakdown.

changes_in_application_order.reason: Break the opening into goal, intentional doping, unwanted metals and product; remove a misleading single-sentence transistor definition.
changes_in_application_order.before: The problem this stage solves is brutally simple to state and brutally hard to do: take silicon dioxide, the most abundant compound in the Earth's crust, and turn it into elemental silicon in which fewer than one atom in a billion is anything other than silicon. A leading-edge transistor does not care that silicon is common. It cares about which foreign atoms sit in the crystal around it. A **dopant** is an impurity added on purpose: boron has one electron fewer than silicon and makes **p-type** silicon, in which current is carried by mobile electron vacancies called holes; phosphorus has one electron more and makes **n-type** silicon, in which current is carried by the spare electrons. A transistor is a switch built from adjacent p-type and n-type regions, so the wafer maker introduces a controlled dopant concentration of perhaps 10^15 atoms per cm³ and needs any residual, uncontrolled boron and phosphorus to be at least a thousand times lower than that. Boron and phosphorus are dangerous precisely because they are dopants: a stray one changes the switch's behaviour. Metals are dangerous for a different reason: an atom of iron, copper, or nickel lodged in the lattice acts as a trap that swallows the free electrons the switch relies on, or as a short through the **gate oxide**, the insulating layer only a few atoms thick that separates the silicon from the transistor's control electrode (its **gate**, the terminal whose voltage turns the switch on and off). The product of this stage is **polycrystalline silicon (polysilicon)**: a solid made of millions of small silicon crystals in random orientations, which is what you get when silicon deposits everywhere at once on a hot rod. A wafer needs one continuous crystal; turning polysilicon into that is Module 02's job.
changes_in_application_order.after:
This stage has a clear goal: take silicon dioxide, the most abundant compound in the Earth's crust, and turn it into elemental silicon in which fewer than one atom in a billion is anything other than silicon.

The amount of silicon is not the difficulty. The difficulty is controlling which foreign atoms remain among its atoms, because different impurities change electrical behaviour in different ways. A **dopant** is an impurity added on purpose: boron has one electron fewer than silicon and makes **p-type** silicon, in which current is carried by mobile electron vacancies called holes; phosphorus has one electron more and makes **n-type** silicon, in which current is carried by the spare electrons. A transistor uses carefully arranged regions of semiconductor to control current, so the wafer maker introduces a controlled dopant concentration of perhaps 10^15 atoms per cm³ and needs any residual, uncontrolled boron and phosphorus to be at least a thousand times lower than that. Boron and phosphorus are dangerous precisely because they are dopants: a stray one changes the switch's behaviour.

Metals cause a different problem: an atom of iron, copper, or nickel lodged in the lattice acts as a trap that swallows the free electrons the switch relies on, or as a short through the **gate oxide**, the insulating layer only a few atoms thick that separates the silicon from the transistor's control electrode (its **gate**, the terminal whose voltage turns the switch on and off).

The product of this stage is **polycrystalline silicon (polysilicon)**: a solid made of millions of small silicon crystals in random orientations, which is what you get when silicon deposits everywhere at once on a hot rod. A wafer needs one continuous crystal; turning polysilicon into that is Module 02's job.

changes_in_application_order.reason: Name all prerequisite equation quantities and separate thermodynamic favourability from speed.
changes_in_application_order.before: - **Heat of reaction.** A reaction's enthalpy change ΔH is the heat it absorbs (positive) or releases (negative). Reactions that turn solids into gases become favourable at high temperature because gas has far more entropy (disorder); the deciding quantity is ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, and the reaction goes when ΔG is negative.
changes_in_application_order.after: - **Heat of reaction.** A reaction's enthalpy change ΔH is the heat it absorbs (positive) or releases (negative). Its entropy change ΔS describes the change in how widely matter and energy can be distributed; producing gas often increases it. The balance is ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, where T is absolute temperature in kelvin and ΔG is the Gibbs free-energy change. A negative ΔG says the reaction is thermodynamically favoured under the stated conditions. It does not say how fast it happens; temperature must also make the reaction fast enough to be useful.

Everything else, the vent-gas recovery, the silicon tetrachloride converter, the HCl absorber, exists to close the mass balance so that chlorine and hydrogen circulate and only silicon leaves. changes_in_application_order.after:
The Siemens process changes silicon's form so it can be separated from its contaminants, then changes it back. First, **metallurgical-grade silicon (MG-Si)** reacts with hydrogen chloride (HCl) to make **trichlorosilane (TCS, SiHCl₃)**. Next, distillation separates this volatile compound from other compounds. Finally, it decomposes on hot silicon rods, leaving purified solid silicon behind. These are the three **unit operations**, meaning the main kinds of processing, in the plant.

The plant also recovers and reuses chemicals. Vent-gas recovery, the silicon tetrachloride converter and the HCl absorber close the **mass balance**: accounting for where each input goes, so chlorine and hydrogen can circulate rather than being discarded after one pass. changes_in_application_order.reason: Explain why grain boundaries matter instead of treating polycrystalline material as universally useless.
changes_in_application_order.before: chemically about as pure as any bulk material humans make, and structurally useless. Polysilicon is a jumble of millimetre-sized grains, each a perfect little crystal pointing in a random direction. A transistor cannot be built across a grain boundary.
changes_in_application_order.after: chemically extremely pure but not yet the structure needed for the wafers in this course. Polysilicon is a jumble of millimetre-sized grains, each a little crystal pointing in a different direction. Where grains meet, the atomic pattern is interrupted. Such **grain boundaries** can trap charge and interfere with predictable current flow, so the active silicon of these wafers must be one continuous crystal.

changes_in_application_order.reason: Bound the filter analogy and distinguish structural defect control from chemical purification.
changes_in_application_order.before: The neck is a filter with nothing for the wrinkle to hide behind: make the rod thin, grow it fast, and every dislocation reaches the surface and leaves.

changes_in_application_order.reason: Clarify that materials can serve both manufacturing and device roles.

changes_in_application_order.after: Materials play two roles in a chip factory: they become part of the finished device, or they help manufacture it. Some do both. **Consumables** are the materials used up or regularly replaced during manufacturing.

changes_in_application_order.reason: Lead with GPU/die/wafer/package relationships before the example inventory; avoid implying every mask transmits light.
changes_in_application_order.before: A single NVIDIA Blackwell GPU package contains two **dies** (a die is one rectangular chip cut from a round silicon wafer) of roughly 800 mm² each, about 208 billion transistors, eight stacks of **high-bandwidth memory (HBM)** (DRAM memory chips stacked on top of one another and placed beside the GPU), and a silicon-and-organic **substrate** (the layered carrier that connects the dies to a circuit board), assembled by more than a dozen companies on three continents. The **package** is the whole assembly of dies, memory, substrate, lid and solder balls: the object that gets soldered to a board. Its silicon was quartz in a mine in Norway, Brazil, or North Carolina roughly a year before the GPU booted. In between, the material passed through something like 1,500 discrete process steps, a **mask set** (the ~100 stencils through which each layer of the chip is printed) that cost tens of millions of dollars, machines that individually sell for $200–400 million, and a **fab** (a chip factory) that cost more than an aircraft carrier. No single person understands every step at the level of the engineers who own it. That is the problem this module solves: you need a map of the whole territory before you walk any part of it, so that when Module 08 spends 7,000 words on tin droplets you know why they matter and where they sit.
changes_in_application_order.after:
Start with the object this course follows: a **GPU**, or graphics processing unit, used here to perform the arithmetic for AI. It is built from silicon chips and supporting parts. A **die** is one rectangular chip cut from a round silicon **wafer**, the shared surface on which many chips are made. The **package** joins dies, memory, a supporting carrier, a lid and solder balls into the object that gets soldered to a circuit board.

A single NVIDIA Blackwell GPU package contains two dies of roughly 800 mm² each, about 208 billion **transistors** (electrically controlled switches), and eight stacks of **high-bandwidth memory (HBM)**. HBM stacks DRAM memory chips, which hold working data, beside the GPU so data can move between them rapidly. A silicon-and-organic **substrate**, the layered carrier, connects the dies to the circuit board. More than a dozen companies on three continents assemble the parts.

Its silicon was quartz in a mine in Norway, Brazil, or North Carolina roughly a year before the GPU booted. In between, the material passed through something like 1,500 discrete process steps, a **mask set** (the ~100 master patterns used to print the chip's layers) that cost tens of millions of dollars, machines that individually sell for $200–400 million, and a **fab** (a chip factory) that cost more than an aircraft carrier. No single person understands every step at the level of the engineers who own it. That is the problem this module solves: you need a map of the whole territory before you walk any part of it, so that when Module 08 spends 7,000 words on tin droplets you know why they matter and where they sit.

changes_in_application_order.reason: Name power equation quantities and connect high current to physical manufacturing.
changes_in_application_order.before: - **Voltage, current, power.** P = V × I. A GPU runs its transistors at about 1 V, so a 1,000 W chip draws ~1,000 A, which is why power delivery is a manufacturing problem and not only an electrical one. (Module 19)
changes_in_application_order.after: - **Voltage, current, power.** Voltage V is the electrical push, current I is the rate of charge flow, and power P is the rate of energy transfer: P = V × I. A GPU runs its transistors at about 1 V, so a 1,000 W chip draws ~1,000 A. Delivering that much current requires substantial connections even though the switches themselves are tiny. (Module 19)

changes_in_application_order.reason: Replace an apparent wavelength cutoff with the blur mechanism and preserve the path to DUV sub-wavelength imaging.
changes_in_application_order.before: - **Light and resolution.** You cannot print a feature much smaller than the wavelength of the light you print it with; shorter wavelength → smaller features. (Module 07)
changes_in_application_order.after: - **Light and resolution.** Light spreads as it passes a patterned mask, so the image on the wafer is blurred rather than a perfect shadow. Shorter wavelengths help resolve finer detail. Lens design, illumination and chemistry also matter: features can be smaller than the wavelength, as Module 07 explains.

changes_in_application_order.reason: Separate production volume from usable output before cost and supply-chain discussion.

changes_in_application_order.after: **Yield** is the fraction of parts that work. It measures success, not production speed: a fast factory can still produce many unusable chips. **Wafer starts per month (wpm)** is how many wafers a fab begins processing each month.

changes_in_application_order.reason: Establish the shaping problem before the specification list and distinguish flatness from roughness.
changes_in_application_order.before: A finished Czochralski ingot is a 300 mm diameter, roughly 2 m long, 300+ kg cylinder of single-crystal silicon with a domed crown on one end and a conical tail on the other. What a fab wants is about 1,500 to 2,000 discs cut from it, each 775 µm thick, with a front surface whose height varies by less than ~20 nm across any 26 mm × 8 mm **lithography site** (the strip of wafer that a lithography scanner images in one sweep of its light slit; Modules 07–08). Scale the wafer up to a football field 100 m across and the allowed bump height within a site is ~7 µm, a tenth of a human hair. The surface must also have roughness below 0.1 nm RMS (**root-mean-square (RMS) roughness** is the typical height of the bumps on a surface; 0.1 nm is less than one atomic layer of silicon, which is 0.136 nm high), fewer than a handful of particles larger than 26 nm across the whole surface, metal contamination below ~10^10 atoms/cm² (a (100) silicon surface holds ~6.8 × 10^14 atoms/cm², so that is one foreign atom per ~70,000 surface silicon atoms), and edges that will not chip during a thousand process steps. Each of these is a specification you will be able to explain by the end of this module.
changes_in_application_order.after:
The crystal grower delivers a solid cylinder; the fab needs thin discs that stay in focus when a pattern is projected onto them. Slicing creates the discs, but sawing alone cannot make the smooth, undamaged surface the fab needs.

A finished Czochralski **ingot**, the cylinder grown from molten silicon, is a 300 mm diameter, roughly 2 m long, 300+ kg cylinder of single-crystal silicon with a domed crown on one end and a conical tail on the other. What a fab wants is about 1,500 to 2,000 discs cut from it, each 775 µm thick, with a front surface whose height varies by less than ~20 nm across any 26 mm × 8 mm **lithography site** (the strip of wafer that a lithography scanner images in one sweep of its light slit; Modules 07–08). Scale the wafer up to a football field 100 m across and the allowed bump height within a site is ~7 µm, a tenth of a human hair.

Flatness and roughness describe different problems. Flatness asks whether a patch of wafer rises or falls across the area being printed. Roughness asks how bumpy the surface is at much smaller scales. A surface can be smoothly curved, like a polished lens, yet fail the wafer's flatness requirement. The surface must also have roughness below 0.1 nm RMS (**root-mean-square (RMS) roughness** is the typical height of the bumps on a surface; 0.1 nm is less than one atomic layer of silicon, which is 0.136 nm high), fewer than a handful of particles larger than 26 nm across the whole surface, metal contamination below ~10^10 atoms/cm² (a (100) silicon surface holds ~6.8 × 10^14 atoms/cm², so that is one foreign atom per ~70,000 surface silicon atoms), and edges that will not chip during a thousand process steps. Each of these is a specification you will be able to explain by the end of this module.

changes_in_application_order.reason: Provide a reader route through the oxidation equation before its coefficient definitions and solution.
changes_in_application_order.before: x² + A x = B (t + τ)
changes_in_application_order.after:
x² + A x = B (t + τ)

Read this first as a relationship between oxide thickness x and growth time t. The constants A and B summarize the reaction and transport conditions; A has units of length and B has units of length squared per time. The offset τ accounts for the starting oxide. At small x the A x term is more important, so thickness grows roughly with time. At large x the x² term dominates, so further growth slows: the reacting molecules must travel through more oxide to reach the silicon.

changes_in_application_order.reason: Explain temporary pattern transfer before resist vocabulary and split pitch, width and placement into digestible ideas.
changes_in_application_order.before: Every layer of a chip begins as a pattern that has to be transferred onto the wafer, and **lithography** is the step that does it: the only process in the fab that *creates* geometry rather than modifying a film already there. Its working material is **photoresist**, a light-sensitive polymer film spun onto the wafer whose solubility in a developer changes wherever light hits it, so that after development the wafer carries a stencil of the design. A chip is a stack of ~60–80+ such patterned **layers**, each needing its own lithography pass. A repeating line pattern is described by its **pitch**, the centre-to-centre distance between neighbouring lines, and its **half-pitch**, half of that, which equals the line width when lines and spaces are equal, so "40 nm half-pitch" and "40 nm lines at 80 nm pitch" are the same statement; the printed width of the smallest feature on a layer is its **critical dimension (CD)**; and **overlay** is how accurately one layer's pattern sits on the layer beneath it. In those words the job is brutal: print 40 nm half-pitch (80 nm pitch) in one exposure and, with multi-patterning, pitches down to ~30–40 nm in production, across a 300 mm wafer, placed within ~1.5–2 nm of the layer underneath, at ~275–300 wafers per hour, 60–80+ times per wafer.
changes_in_application_order.after:
To build a circuit, the fab must decide where material will stay and where it will be removed or changed. **Lithography** writes that location information as a temporary pattern on the wafer. Later processing transfers the pattern into a more durable material. Its working material is **photoresist**, a light-sensitive polymer film spun onto the wafer whose ability to dissolve changes after exposure to light. A liquid called the **developer** removes the soluble regions, leaving a temporary stencil of the design.

A chip is a stack of ~60–80+ such patterned **layers**, each needing its own lithography pass.

A repeating line pattern is described by its **pitch**, the centre-to-centre distance between neighbouring lines, and its **half-pitch**, half of that, which equals the line width when lines and spaces are equal, so "40 nm half-pitch" and "40 nm lines at 80 nm pitch" are the same statement. The printed width of the smallest feature on a layer is its **critical dimension (CD)**. **Overlay** is how accurately one layer's pattern sits on the layer beneath it. These measure different things: a line can have the right width but be in the wrong place. The production task is to print 40 nm half-pitch (80 nm pitch) in one exposure and, with multi-patterning, pitches down to ~30–40 nm in production, across a 300 mm wafer, placed within ~1.5–2 nm of the layer underneath, at ~275–300 wafers per hour, 60–80+ times per wafer.
